## Problem 1.

### 1.1 Building birthday function

```{r}
birthday_repeated = function(n_room) {

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_room, replace = TRUE)

  repeated_bday = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_room

  repeated_bday

}
```

### 1.2 Testing birthday function

```{r}
birthday_repeated(10)
```

### 1.3 Applying birthday function to n = 2:50, 10,000 times. 

```{r}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    number_of_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(number_of_people, birthday_repeated)
  ) |>
  group_by(number_of_people) |>
  summarize(prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated))
```

### Plot 1: Probability of a shared birthday as a function of group size.

```{r}
birthday_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = number_of_people, y = prob_of_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability that at least two people share a birthday",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday"
  )
```

```{r}
first_over_half =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(prob_of_repeat > 0.5) |>
  pull(number_of_people) |>
  min()

prob_23 =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(number_of_people == 23) |>
  pull(prob_of_repeat)

prob_50 =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(number_of_people == 50) |>
  pull(prob_of_repeat)
```

The probability that at least two people share a birthday increases quickly and non-linearly with group size. It is close to 0 for very small groups, but by around group size of `r first_over_half` it goes above 50% (estimated mean = `r round(prob_23, 3)`). By a group size of 50, the estimated probability is `r round(prob_50, 3)`, so a shared birthday is almost certain. This is much higher than most people would guess, because the number of possible pairs of people grows much faster than the number of people.

## Problem 2

### 2.1: Import data

```{r, message = FALSE}
study_df = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |> 
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)) |> 
  unnest(data) |> 
  mutate(files = str_remove(files, ".csv")) |> 
  separate(files, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |> 
  mutate(
    arm = case_match(
      arm, 
      "con" ~ "control", 
      "exp" ~ "experimental"
    )
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(arm, subject_id, week, observation)

study_df
```

The tidy dataset has `r nrow(study_df)` rows, with one row per subject per week (8 weeks total), and `r n_distinct(str_c(study_df$arm, study_df$subject_id))` subjects in total -- 10 subjects per arm. 

### 2.2 Spaghetti plot

```{r}
study_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = str_c(arm, subject_id), color = arm)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d((end = 0.9)) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations on each subject over time",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```


```{r}
arm_means_df = 
  study_df |> 
  filter(week %in% c(1, 8)) |> 
  group_by(arm, week) |> 
  summarize(mean_obs = mean(observation), .groups = "drop")

con_wk1 = arm_means_df |> 
  filter(arm == "control", week == 1) |>
  pull(mean_obs)

con_wk8 = arm_means_df |> 
  filter(arm == "control", week == 8) |> 
  pull(mean_obs)

exp_wk1 = arm_means_df |> 
  filter(arm == "experimental", week == 1) |> 
  pull(mean_obs)

exp_wk8 = arm_means_df |> 
  filter(arm == "experimental", week == 8) |> 
  pull(mean_obs)
```

At week 1, the two arms look similar, with a mean observation of 
`r round(con_wk1, 2)` in the control arm and `r round(exp_wk1, 2)` in the 
experimental arm. Over the 8 weeks, observations in the control arm stay roughly flat until it slightly decreases towards week 8 (mean = `r round(con_wk8, 2)`). In contrast, observations in the experimental arm increase steadily over time, reaching a mean of `r round(exp_wk8, 2)` at week 8. By the end of the study, nearly all experimental subjects have higher values than control subjects. There is also substantial week-to-week variability within subjects in both arms. 

It is important to note that some observations are negative, mostly in the control arm. However, since the homework does not describe what is being measured, these values were kept as recorded.

## Problem 3

### 3.1: building function

```{r}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data =
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    )

  t.test(sim_data |> pull(x), mu = 0, conf.level = 0.95) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)

}
```

### 3.2 Testing function

```{r}
sim_t_test(mu = 0)
```

### 3.3 Generate 5000 datasets from the model

```{r}
sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    est_df = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)
  ) |>
  unnest(est_df) |>
  mutate(rejected = p_value < 0.05)
```

###. 3.4 Plot 3: Proportion of times the null was rejected vs. true mean


```{r}
power_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(power = mean(rejected))

power_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Power of the one-sample t-test by true mean",
    x = "True value of mu",
    y = "Proportion of times the null was rejected"
  )
```

Power increases as the effect size increases. When mu = 0, the null is true and it is rejected `r power_df |> filter(true_mu == 0) |> pull(power)` of the time, which is close to alpha = 0.05 as expected. Power is low for small effects (`r power_df |> filter(true_mu == 1) |> pull(power)` when mu = 1), increases quickly for moderate effects (`r power_df |> filter(true_mu == 3) |> pull(power)` when mu = 3), and is essentially 1 for large effects (`r power_df |> filter(true_mu == 6) |> pull(power)` when mu = 6). Because n and sigma are fixed, a larger true mean is further from the null value of 0, which makes the difference easier to detect and increases power.
